title: Observability Stack
description: The stack watching itself: Prometheus, Loki, Alertmanager and the Alloy agents, plus scrape health for every target. All from metrics the stack already collects — see docs/observability.md.

panels.title: Stack alerts
panels.description: Firing and pending alerts carrying component=stack, from the ALERTS series Prometheus exposes for its own rules. Empty is the good state. Silences live in Alertmanager and are not reflected here — see dashboards/README.md.

options.content:
**A remote-writing agent's `up` goes stale, not to zero.** Prometheus scrapes nine jobs directly; four more (`*-metrics`, `*-alloy`, `integrations/cadvisor`) arrive by remote_write from an Alloy agent that scrapes *itself* and pushes. When one of those agents dies it stops pushing, so its `up` series ages out rather than falling to `0` — and `InstanceDown` is `up == 0`. **For those jobs the staleness panel below, not the Up column, is what the eye reads**, and `RemoteWriteJobStale` is the rule that covers them. It is deliberately not a threshold on that panel: `time() - timestamp(up) > 300` cannot fire for any input, because an instant selector stops returning a sample once the lookback delta passes. It asks instead which jobs were reporting in the last 24 hours and are not reporting now.

**`component=stack` covers six rules.** Five read a component reporting on its own working — a reload rejected, an evaluation failed, a notification undelivered — and none of those can see a component that has stopped publishing altogether. `RemoteWriteJobStale` is the sixth and covers exactly that, for pushed jobs. For the stack's own scraped components it is still `up == 0`, and for the notification path itself it is the Watchdog, because a stack cannot report its own total absence — see the dead man's switch in `docs/observability.md`.

**Alertmanager silences are invisible here.** The alert table reads `ALERTS`, which Prometheus exposes for its own rules and which knows nothing about Alertmanager. A silenced alert still shows as firing.

panels.title: Targets up
panels.description: Fraction of all up series reading 1 — scraped and remote-written alike. Anything below 100% means a target the stack believes it is collecting is not answering.

panels.title: TSDB head series
panels.description: Active series in the head block. The cardinality budget: docs/observability.md sizes retention from this.

panels.title: Samples ingested/s
panels.description: Appended to the head block per second, all sources.

panels.title: Log lines/s into Loki
panels.description: What LokiIngestionStalled fires on when it reaches zero for 30 minutes.

panels.title: Remote-write lag
panels.description: Newest sample an Alloy agent holds, minus the newest it has confirmed sent. Climbing means remote_write is failing or throttled — this is the panel that would have shown #12's stale address immediately.

panels.title: Notification failures (24h)
panels.description: Deliveries Alertmanager could not make. Non-zero means alerts fired and reached nobody.

panels.title: Every target
panels.description: Every up series the stack holds, with how long its scrape took and how many samples it returned. Samples is the column that matters: cAdvisor reporting one series where it should report hundreds is invisible in Up and obvious here (#12). Remote-written jobs show their last pushed value, which is why Staleness sits beside it.

panels.title: Samples returned per scrape
panels.description: How many samples each target returns. A step change here is a collector that has stopped exporting most of what it used to — the cAdvisor fault in #12 was a drop from hundreds to one, with up staying 1 throughout.

panels.title: Scrape duration by target
panels.description: Time each scrape took. The snmp job runs a 45s timeout against the iLO's ~1,600-metric module, so it sits far above the rest by design.

panels.title: Sample staleness by job
panels.description: Now, minus the timestamp of each job's most recent up sample. For directly scraped jobs this hugs the scrape interval. For remote-written jobs it is what the eye reads for liveness: a dead agent's series ages out rather than falling to 0, so InstanceDown (up == 0) cannot see it and RemoteWriteJobStale is the rule that can. Read as a 10-minute maximum: instantaneously this sawtooths between 0 and the scrape interval on every healthy target, which draws as a solid block and hides the one line that is climbing.

panels.title: TSDB head
panels.description: Series and chunks held in the head block. Every panel here is filtered to job=prometheus on purpose: Alloy and Loki export prometheus_tsdb_* about their own WALs, and unfiltered these return three series from three different processes.

panels.title: Sample ingestion
panels.description: Samples appended to the head per second. The sum() is required rather than cosmetic — Prometheus 3 splits this counter by a type label (float and histogram), so the bare rate returns two series.

panels.title: WAL and on-disk blocks
panels.description: WAL segment number and the size of the persisted blocks. Blocks bytes is what PROMETHEUS_RETENTION_SIZE caps at 12 GiB; PrometheusSizeRetentionActive fires when that ceiling starts evicting, which silently shortens retention below the documented 30 days.

panels.title: Rule evaluation
panels.description: How long each rule group takes, against its own interval. Groups whose duration approaches their interval start missing iterations, which is what iterations_missed counts. PrometheusRuleEvaluationFailures fires on the failure counter.

panels.title: Ingestion
panels.description: Lines and bytes the distributor accepted. The lines series reaching zero for 30 minutes is exactly what LokiIngestionStalled fires on — a rule that had nothing charting it until #81.

panels.title: Chunks and streams
panels.description: Streams and chunks held in memory, and the rate at which chunks are flushed to disk. Streams is the cardinality figure for logs — docs/observability.md's rule about never promoting a request ID or IP to a label is about keeping this number bounded.

panels.title: Requests by route and status
panels.description: Every HTTP route Loki serves, split by status code. Pushes arriving from Alloy and queries coming from Grafana are both here; a 4xx or 5xx on loki_api_v1_push is log data being rejected rather than queued.

panels.title: Ruler evaluation
panels.description: The Loki ruler's own evaluation timing and failures. Note the metric prefix: on Loki 3.7 these are loki_prometheus_rule_*, not the cortex_prometheus_rule_* the upstream docs suggest and not loki_ruler_* — guessing either returns no data at all.

panels.title: Notifications by integration
panels.description: Deliveries attempted per receiver integration. All four destinations are webhooks, so integration reads webhook for each — the receiver names are in docs/observability.md's routing table. Flat at zero is normal; the Watchdog's own 5-minute heartbeat is the one series that should never be. Alertmanager registers a series for every integration it supports, not only the ones configured, so this is guarded to the integrations that have actually sent something in the last 24 hours — otherwise 17 flat-zero lines bury the one that matters.

panels.title: Notification failures by integration
panels.description: Deliveries that errored. AlertmanagerNotificationsFailing fires on this. It cannot see a webhook that is well-formed, reachable and pointed at nothing — a 200 into a deleted topic is a success by every measure Alertmanager has, which is what the Watchdog exists for (#67). Alertmanager registers a series for every integration it supports, not only the ones configured, so this is guarded to the integrations that have actually sent something in the last 24 hours — otherwise 17 flat-zero lines bury the one that matters.

panels.title: Alerts by state
panels.description: What Alertmanager currently holds. Suppressed counts alerts hidden by a silence or an inhibit rule — the difference between this and the alert table at the top of this dashboard is precisely the silences, which ALERTS knows nothing about.

panels.title: Silences and config reloads
panels.description: Silences by state, and whether the last config reload was accepted. docs/observability.md records every deliberate silence by UUID and expiry in three places; a count here that the docs do not account for is a silence somebody forgot to write down.

panels.title: Remote-write throughput
panels.description: Samples each agent has shipped to Prometheus, and how many failed. Since #81 every agent scrapes itself and pushes its own internals, so this covers oracle as well as the monitoring host — before that it covered one agent of two and the #12 remote_write fault was invisible on the other.

panels.title: Remote-write lag and backlog
panels.description: Lag is the newest sample held minus the newest confirmed sent. Pending is what is queued behind it. Both climbing while failed/s stays flat is a receiver accepting slowly; both climbing with failures is a receiver that has gone away.

targets.expr: max by (job) (prometheus_remote_storage_highest_timestamp_in_seconds{job=~"alloy|.+-alloy"} - ignoring(component_id, component_path, remote_name, url) prometheus_remote_storage_queue_highest_sent_timestamp_seconds{job=~"alloy|.+-alloy"})

panels.title: Component health
panels.description: Alloy's own components, by the health it reports for each. Anything outside healthy means a component is loaded but not working — a log source whose file vanished, or an exporter that cannot reach its socket. config_last_load_successful going to 0 means the file on disk was rejected and the agent is running the previous one.

panels.title: Log lines forwarded by writer
panels.description: Lines each loki.write component has shipped, and any it dropped. The two writers are deliberate: grafana_loki stamps host from the agent's own hostname, network_syslog does not, so relayed pfSense lines keep host=morpheus instead of being labelled with the agent that relayed them.

panels.title: WAL size and append rate
panels.description: What each agent is holding in its write-ahead log, and how fast it is going in. The WAL is where samples wait between being scraped and being confirmed sent, so active series climbing while Remote-write throughput's sent/s stays flat is a receiver that is not draining what the agent is writing. That backlog is bounded by disk rather than by memory, which is why it shows here as growth rather than as an agent falling over.

panels.title: WAL replay and corruption
panels.description: Replay is how long the agent spent reading its own WAL back at startup, so this only moves when an agent restarts — a step in it dates a restart to the minute, which is the context missing when Remote-write lag jumps and nothing says why. Corruptions are samples the WAL could not read back at all: non-zero means those samples are already lost, and no retry recovers them.
